steelman: A company rebrand can involve more than a logo change: cloud account restructuring such as billing account migration, organizational hierarchy changes, or resource retagging could inadvertently reset quota tiers or alter effective rate limits on a storage bucket. If the rebrand involved CDN reconfiguration or a custom domain update for the storage endpoint, uploads might land on a backend with stricter per-client throttle limits. A rebrand could also spin up new resources sharing quota pools with existing infrastructure, introducing contention. Finally, a coincident cloud provider maintenance window timed to the public launch could have altered default limits. A cautious SRE should at minimum verify whether any cloud-account-level changes accompanied the brand launch.
notes: The xbase explicitly states 'The bucket name and IAM credentials are unchanged,' which forecloses every defensible mechanism: same IAM credentials means the account tier and quota context are unaltered; same bucket name means no DNS/CDN/endpoint reconfiguration redirected uploads to a different backend. A communications-layer rebrand (new name and logo) with no cloud-infrastructure changes has no pathway to alter server-side request rate enforcement. The seed is clean on this lens. The curator's own causal_audit field reaches the same conclusion (steelman_verdict: no_defensible_mechanism), consistent with this independent finding.
